To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we used independent components analysis to characterize functional networks for cognitive control and found that these networks were temporally sorted for stop success and stop error trials.

1) ICA identified a network of functional networks that were temporally ordered for go success, stop success (SS), and stop error (se) trials in the stop signal task, 2) the event associated weights for the functional networks showed a pattern of correlation across subjects that is distinct for the go success and stop error events and is similar for the stop success and stop error, 3) the pattern of correlation for go success and stop success is consistent with a model of cognitive control

we used ICA to characterize the functional networks subserving cognitive processes in the stop signal task, and that the event associated weights for these functional networks showed distinct patterns of correlation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control.
the cognitive processes that underlie the ability to stop an ongoing action.
the cognitive and neural mechanisms of cognitive control, the executive function of the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cognitive control is a complex process, which is mediated by a network of brain regions that are not limited to the frontal lobe, but also include parietal regions and the basal ganglia.
cognitive control is a critical and complex executive function of the brain.
the brain is a network of networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cognitive control is a complex function that requires the coordination of multiple neural systems.
the ICA method is a very useful tool to study cognitive control in fMRI data.
the stop signal task is a complex cognitive control task that engages multiple functional networks, and that these networks interact in a coordinated way to achieve successful performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cognitive control, the executive function of the brain, is not one thing.
we were able to use independent component analysis (a data driven method) to elucidate the neural networks subserving the component processes of the stop signal task.
cognitive control can be characterized by six distinct functional networks, each of which can be temporally sorted for stop signal success and stop signal failure trials.
